# Excerpt library: how the winners say each kind of thing

Short lines from winning BeardedViking (BV) and WhosTheVoss (Voss) scripts, grouped by the job the line does. Each one shows its source as channel · video · timestamp · the video's views against its channel normal.

**Sources:** 25 transcripts (in `archive/`), 16 of them at 4x or more their channel normal. Every group holds 10-15 lines from at least 6 different videos, mostly from the 4x-and-up videos, and every line in a group is a different shape. Quotes are verbatim auto-captions (caption mishearings such as "naughty pine" are kept and noted); the timestamp is where the quote starts.

**How to use this file:** to learn the range of shapes each kind of line can take, never to copy wording. Every group deliberately holds several different shapes. Pick a different shape from the last script on the same channel, and write it fresh in the persona's voice.

**Transfer notes:**
- **✓ shape works as-is**
- **✎ rewrite needed** (usually a first-person claim turned into an instruction or an opinion)
- **✗ doesn't transfer** (it only works because a real person built the thing on camera)

## Contents
1. Promise lines (the opening)
2. Materials and where to buy
3. Tool alternatives and optional steps
4. Step lines: short, medium, long, and batching
5. Tips and safety inside the step
6. Candor
7. Money: listing proof, price, cost, what's left, listing angle
8. The doubter
9. Adversaries
10. Where to sell
11. The final content beat
12. Hook-to-first-material transitions
13. Short bridges between steps
14. Finish lines
15. Mid-video CTAs (shape only)

---

## 1. Promise lines

The opening line or two: what the build turns into, before any material is named.

1. "Two boards turned into 37 products, turning your hobby into additional income for these coming holidays." [BV · 2 tools paid my bills · 0:00 · 1.8x]
   ✓ **Shape:** material count → product count → outcome, with a seasonal hook.
2. "Two 2x4s transformed into 170 products, turning enough profit for you to buy every major tool for your shop." [Voss · This ONE Project · 0:00 · 10.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the yield count turned into one title-sized purchase goal, framed as what *you* could buy. A close relative of 1; pick one or the other, never both on one channel in a row.
3. "Today I'm going to show you how to build one simple project from one 1x4x8 and make $100. Let's go." [BV · hotcakes · 0:00 · 15.8x]
   ✎ Plain and fast, but "today I'm going to show you" is a banned opener and "make $100" reads as a guarantee → "Here's one simple build from a single 1x4x8 that could turn into up to a hundred dollars."
4. "Today's build takes less time than cooking a Jack's pizza. It's an easy sell on Facebook Marketplace, cost-friendly to ship on Etsy, and its ability to be personalized is why you can name your price." [Voss · ZERO CUTS · 0:00 · 4.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** an everyday time comparison, then three quick reasons it sells. (BV's version, "less time than walking my dog," is personal: ✗.)
5. "I'm really not sure how people turn a profit on these massive organizers. I have a better product that only takes 10 minutes, requires two 2x4s…" [Voss · I still don't understand · 0:00 · 8.3x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a contrarian opinion, then the better option. An opinion, not a biography.
6. "No matter what you're building in your shop, you're going to have sawdust afterwards. Let's turn it into some going out to eat money." [Voss · Sawdust · 0:00 · 11.5x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a universal situation, then a small, concrete money purpose.
7. "With the weather warming up and the local markets picking up steam, it's about that time to get in your shop and start building. Okay, Daniel, but what am I going to build?" [BV · So many orders · 0:00 · 8.6x]
   ✓ **Shape:** season timing, then the doubter asks the question the video answers. A named doubter is a persona-profile decision.
8. "Two boards, totaling less than $15 in production costs, build six of these and you'll be able to buy yourself an airline ticket to anywhere you want to go." [BV · wife · 0:00 · 12.7x]
   ✎ **Shape:** cost → batch → a tangible reward. Make it conditional → "Two boards and under fifteen dollars in material: build six, and if they sell, that could cover a plane ticket."
9. "Every one of you has a cell phone either in your hand, in your pocket or in front of you right now, and this accessory could make you more money than a US Governor salary." [Voss · 19 products · 0:00 · 9.2x]
   ✎ **Shape:** the object already in the viewer's hand, then an outsized comparison. The comparison has to be one the money block can reach with honest math, and never a promise → "Nearly everyone watching has a phone within arm's reach, and a simple stand for it could, if a few sell each day, out-earn a part-time job."
10. "Selling for one Hamilton, I still pocket $100 off the first board. On the second board that number jumps to $160 and so on." [Voss · I buy ALL the tools · 0:14 · 4.2x]
    ✎ **Shape:** an escalation ladder: the first batch carries the tool cost, the next one doesn't. "I pocket" is a personal sales claim and the Hamilton line is a gag → "Listed around ten dollars, the first board could clear the tool costs and still leave about a hundred; from the second board on, the tool money stays with you too."
11. "I've been showing beginner woodworkers how to build simple projects and turn their hobby into extra income without using any kind of fancy tools or expensive equipment." [BV · Truck · 0:00 · 39.4x]
    ✗ A track-record opener: it's the narrator's own history and works as a channel intro, both banned. What survives is the "no fancy tools" reassurance, said once about this build.
12. "This thing is in 32 people's carts and 35 have been sold in the last 24 hours." [BV · 32 products · 0:24 · 7.1x]
    ✎ **Shape:** a live demand signal straight from a marketplace listing. Use it only when the pack holds that listing's own counts, and say what the listing shows instead of pointing → "One listing for this stand showed thirty-five sold in a single day, with dozens more sitting in shoppers' carts."
13. "It is no secret that when the springtime comes around the local markets get flooded with planners and super oversaturated. So, for our first project, I'm going to show you how to combat that and build a planner that nobody else is building." [BV · Non stop orders · 0:14 · 6.4x]
    ✎ **Shape:** a saturated market, then the version that stands apart. (The captions read "planners" for planters.) "Nobody else is building" can't be proven, and "I'm going to show you" is a banned opener → "Every spring the market tables fill up with the same planters, so this one is built to look different from the rest of the row."
14. "These are three projects every beginner should be building." [BV · 4 beginner projects · 0:00 · 4.9x]
    ✓ **Shape:** a "should" aimed at a named audience. The channel intro that follows it in the source is banned; the "should" line stands alone.
15. "Here's what you're going to need. One board, five masonry cut nails, some natural fiber rope, a few basic power tools, coffee included, and no fancy shop required." [BV · student loan · 0:04 · 5.6x]
    ✎ **Shape:** the short kit list as the promise: the shortness of the list is the selling point. Drop the coffee gag → "All it takes: a single 2x4, five cut nails, a length of natural rope and the basic power tools most garages already have."

## 2. Materials and where to buy

1. "Slide up to Lowe's and grab yourself a 1x4x8 for around eight bucks." [BV · hotcakes · 0:08 · 15.8x]
   ✓ **Shape:** store, board, price, in one breath.
2. "First things first, you'll want to head up to Lowe's and grab yourself some 1x4x8, which is going to run you approximately anywhere from 6 to 8 bucks." [BV · sell fast · 0:17 · 11.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the price given as a range.
3. "Head to your nearest big box store and pick up a 1x12x8 and a 1x3x10 costing right around $30, $35. Prices subject to change." [BV · 2 tools paid my bills · 0:05 · 1.8x]
   ✓ **Shape:** two boards under one combined price, then "prices subject to change" once, straight after the prices.
4. "You're going to grab one board totaling around $4.65, which is a 2 by 4 by 8. You may have to cull through these, but it'll be worth it in the long run to get the straightest one." [BV · Truck · 0:14 · 39.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** price, then a selection tip.
5. "If you have a piece of scrap laying around, or if you just head over to your big box store, a lot of times you can buy them in 2-ft and 4-ft lengths, so you don't have to dedicate yourself to a full 8-ft piece." [Voss · This Viral Toy · 11:37 · 1.5x]
   ✓ **Shape:** buy less of it: scrap, or a shorter length.
6. "Or you can get the furring strip like I typically do for around four bucks." [BV · hotcakes · 0:15 · 15.8x]
   ✎ **Shape:** a cheaper substitute product. Keep the alternative and drop "like I typically do" → "or grab a furring strip for around four."
7. "Now, you could just purchase a 1 by 8 by 8, and that's going to run you right around $17. So, I went with this route because it was the cheaper route." [BV · So many orders · 0:50 · 8.6x]
   ✎ **Shape:** the obvious buy against a cheaper workaround, both priced. "I went with" is the narrator's own shopping trip; make it an opinion → "A ready-made 1x8 costs around seventeen; ripping one from a cheaper panel saves a few dollars, and that's the route I'd take."
8. "We'll calculate this at about 75 cents of stain needed for this project." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 1:24 · 9.2x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the one-project share of a consumable you buy by the can.
9. "And if you're a woodworker, most likely you've already got some stain laying around your shop." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 1:14 · 9.2x]
   ✓ **Shape:** assume they already own it, hedged with "most likely," so the shopping list stays short.
10. "And don't forget to pick up whatever kind of color finishes you want to use for your projects. Adding different colors always helps with the sellability of your projects." [BV · Truck · 0:37 · 39.4x]
    ✓ **Shape:** an open-choice item with a selling reason attached.
11. "Then head down to your electrical aisle, and what you're going to want to grab are these conduit clamps." [BV · 4 beginner projects · 5:35 · 4.9x]
    ✎ **Shape:** aisle directions for an item that isn't in the lumber section. "These" points at footage; name the item instead → "From there, walk over to the electrical aisle for half-inch conduit clamps, the kind with a screw hole on each side."
12. "Lowe's, Home Depot, Menards, all of those will have pine, and a select few are going to have acacia." [Voss · ZERO CUTS · 0:51 · 4.0x]
    ✓ **Shape:** which stores stock which species, so the viewer knows what to expect before the drive. Naming stores is fine; saying anything negative about one isn't.
13. "During your big box store adventure, you're going to look around for one of these, lazy Susan hardware, turntable hardware, rotating tray hardware. It goes by a whole bunch of different names." [Voss · ZERO CUTS · 2:05 · 4.0x]
    ✎ **Shape:** every name the item hides under on the shelf. Drop "one of these" (pointing) → "On the same trip, find the lazy Susan bearing; the label may call it turntable or rotating tray hardware instead."
14. "…select Pine, didn't go with standard cuz those look like they had been chewed up by a dog." [Voss · I buy ALL the tools · 0:59 · 4.2x]
    ✎ **Shape:** which grade to buy, and why. The source is his own shopping trip; turn it into an opinion → "Pay a little more for select pine here; on a piece this small, the standard boards are usually too rough to bother with."
15. "Second ingredient you'll need is some paraffin wax. Comes in these hard little blocks." [Voss · Sawdust · 1:16 · 11.5x]
    ✓ **Shape:** a numbered ingredient, then a plain description of an item the viewer may not know. Describe it ("it comes in hard blocks"); don't point at it.

## 3. Tool alternatives and optional steps

1. "If you don't have a roundover bit, no worries because this is totally optional and it's just for aesthetics." [BV · student loan · 7:36 · 5.6x]
   ✓ **Shape:** optional, and only for looks.
2. "You could either do a 45° miter, or you can set your saw to a 45° bevel." [BV · Truck · 2:06 · 39.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** two saw settings to the same cut.
3. "You can easily knock this build out using only a circular saw." [Voss · I still don't understand · 0:28 · 8.3x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the minimum-tool reassurance, early.
4. "If you want to bypass the whole plug thing, what you could do is head to Lowe's and grab yourself a 3/8 in dowel, and that usually costs right around a dollar to $2." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 8:37 · 9.2x]
   ✓ **Shape:** buy the part instead of making it, with a price.
5. "Make sure you're holding your drill nice and plumb and if you need to, you can use a speed square or they make one of these portable drill presses for your drill that actually attaches to it." [BV · student loan · 5:20 · 5.6x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a free fix, plus an inexpensive gadget option.
6. "No fancy miter saw station with a built-in stop block, no problem." [BV · student loan · 1:00 · 5.6x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the missing setup waved off ("no problem"), then the plain substitute (here, a clamp as the stop block).
7. "If your saw is incapable of going up to a 50° bevel, no worries because a 45° bevel will work just as well." [BV · So many orders · 1:56 · 8.6x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the nearest setting the viewer's tool does reach. Only if the pack confirms the fallback works.
8. "If you don't want to risk overcutting, you could even use a jigsaw or you could even use your band saw. Out of these three options, I like the miter saw because it leaves a cleaner look." [BV · hotcakes · 4:23 · 15.8x]
   ✓ **Shape:** three tools for one cut, ranked, with a preference and its reason. "I like" is an opinion, which is allowed.
9. "If you're trying to figure out how to get this done using just a circular saw or jigsaw, don't worry about the angled fanciness. Just cut them at 90." [Voss · This Viral Toy · 0:47 · 1.5x]
   ✓ **Shape:** drop a decorative feature so the simpler tool can do the job.
10. "If you don't have a band saw, just keep the pieces long after you cut the notch. And you can take care of that with the jigsaw a little bit easier." [BV · 4 beginner projects · 3:54 · 4.9x]
    ✓ **Shape:** change the order of operations so the simpler tool has something to hold on to.
11. "Doing it this way will require some 3/8 inch dowel or you could even make your own plugs. The other option is to use a Kreg Jig and fasten your 2 by 4s from the bottom." [BV · wife · 7:17 · 12.7x]
    ✎ **Shape:** two joinery routes, each with what it requires. "This way" leans on the footage; name both methods → "Screwing down from the top means plugging the holes, with store-bought dowel or plugs you cut yourself; a pocket-hole jig from underneath hides the screws altogether."
12. "Now, once you get these two glued together, if you wanted to, you could add some kind of fastener like a brad nail, or you could even add some screws if you're worried about the glue not holding up…" [BV · Truck · 5:01 · 39.4x]
    ✓ **Shape:** optional reinforcement for the viewer who doesn't trust the glue yet.
13. "Adding that light dusting of sawdust to the top is not a necessary step. However, since these are little fire starters, it does help to ignite the puck, and it dresses them up a little bit." [Voss · Sawdust · 4:59 · 11.5x]
    ✓ **Shape:** an optional step that earns its place twice: once for function, once for looks.
14. "There are multiple ways that you can add a saying or graphic to your project. Let's go from the cheapest to the most expensive." [Voss · ZERO CUTS · 3:23 · 4.0x]
    ✓ **Shape:** an options ladder, ordered by cost.
15. "And if you do own a miter saw, you can get these cut out twice as fast." [Voss · I still don't understand · 0:59 · 8.3x]
    ✎ **Shape:** the upgrade path: what the bigger tool buys you (here, speed). The joke that follows in the source goes; keep the method → "Own a miter saw? Stack two boards tight against the fence and cut both in one pass."

## 4. Step lines

**Short (a few words):**

1. "Flip them around." [BV · sell fast · 8:37 · 11.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a two-word reposition between longer lines.
2. "Blow off all that dust." [BV · sell fast · 8:18 · 11.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a cleanup step done in four words.
3. "45°." [BV · hotcakes · 4:10 · 15.8x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the bare setting, number only, straight after the line that sets it up.
4. "Flush to the bottom." [BV · Non stop orders · 5:23 · 6.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a fragment that gives only the alignment target, no verb.

**Medium:**

5. "With our miter saw set to 90°, now it's time to make our 18 cuts." [BV · wife · 1:11 · 12.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the setting, then the count of cuts it covers.
6. "Work your way through the grit, starting with 80 grit, working your way to 120, and then ultimately finish at 220." [BV · wife · 3:57 · 12.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a progression spelled out start to finish.
7. "Add glue to the end of your 16-in piece, plop it into place, and screw it together, repeating all the way down the line." [Voss · I still don't understand · 2:36 · 8.3x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a three-verb chain that ends by telling you to repeat it.
8. "At the end of your 2x4, measure down 3/4 of an inch and draw a soft line." [Voss · 19 products · 1:09 · 9.2x]
   ✓ **Shape:** measure and mark: a place, a measurement, and how to draw it.

**Long or tricky:**

9. "My first cut is at 8 in, so I'm going to add 5 in onto my measurement to take into account the distance from the base of my saw to my blade." [Voss · I still don't understand · 0:32 · 8.3x]
   ✎ **Shape:** a measurement with the correction that makes it work. Make it an instruction → "Add five inches to every mark to allow for the distance from the edge of the saw's base to the blade."
10. "Where I just made that mark, I take my speed square and put it up against there, but I'm not drawing a line, because that means I'm going to have to erase a line later on." [Voss · I still don't understand · 2:06 · 8.3x]
    ✎ **Shape:** what not to do, with the reason. Drop the "I" and "where I just made" → "Set the speed square on the mark as a guide but skip the pencil line, so there's nothing to erase later."
11. "I'll grab a squeeze clamp, and I'm going to be setting myself up with a stop block right at that 5 and 3/4-in mark we made." [BV · Truck · 1:35 · 39.4x]
    ✎ **Shape:** a jig set-up told as one action. First-person build narration → "Clamp a stop block at the five and three-quarter mark."

**Batching (collapsing repeats):**

12. "Now, just rinse and repeat for all five of those pieces." [BV · student loan · 6:28 · 5.6x]
    ✓ **Shape:** repeat for a stated count.
13. "Then you're going to flip your project over and repeat for this other side." [Voss · I still don't understand · 3:09 · 8.3x]
    ✓ **Shape:** a mirror repeat on the opposite face.
14. "Now, instead of measuring and marking every single one of these like we did this first one, we can just use this as a template." [Voss · This ONE Project · 6:07 · 10.0x]
    ✓ **Shape:** the first finished piece becomes the template. It doubles as a tip.
15. "Now, while we let those pieces dry, we're going to be productive and get our next set of four cut." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 5:11 · 9.2x]
    ✓ **Shape:** use the drying time for the next batch of parts.

## 5. Tips and safety inside the step

1. "Anytime that you're using a stop block setup, you want to make sure to either let that blade stop completely before releasing the saw or just hold down that right side. That way, you avoid the kickback factor." [BV · Truck · 1:46 · 39.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the safety line lives in the step, with the reason.
2. "Don't forget to blow off all that excess dust. You don't want this dust to interfere with the finish." [BV · wife · 4:06 · 12.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a quality tip, then its reason.
3. "Now, when you're using spray paint, you definitely want to make sure to wear a mask." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 8:08 · 9.2x]
   ✓ **Shape:** protective gear in one line, at the moment it applies.
4. "A little painter's tape on the open side of your saw blade really cuts down the amount of sawdust it's kicking back at you." [Voss · This ONE Project · 1:24 · 10.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a cheap shop trick.
5. "See, my fingers are at least 3 and 1/2 in away from that blade." [BV · 32 products · 2:08 · 7.1x]
   ✗ It points at footage of his own hands. The instruction survives: "Keep your fingers at least three and a half inches from the blade."
6. "Use a dot of super glue or wood glue on the bottom of your hole so that way that dowel rod can't fall out or be a choking hazard." [Voss · This ONE Project · 7:15 · 10.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** safety for the end user (here, a child), inside the glue-up step where the risk is made.
7. "A quick tip, whenever measuring from the right side of your board, you want to be sure to cut on the left side of your mark and vice versa. That way you get the accurate measurement you're aiming for." [BV · wife · 0:54 · 12.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** an accuracy rule of thumb, flagged as a tip.
8. "If you notice on your cut nails, these things are pretty thick, so you want to give that a pilot hole that way you don't split your wood." [BV · Truck · 9:03 · 39.4x]
   ✎ **Shape:** a damage-prevention step, with the cause. "If you notice … these things" points at footage → "Cut nails are thick, so drill a pilot hole first or the board will split."
9. "When using your jigsaw, instead of pushing the front in the direction you want it to go, gently drive it from the back. This keeps your blade nice and upright, gives you a nice clean cut." [Voss · This Viral Toy · 3:06 · 1.5x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a technique correction ("instead of X, do Y"), then the result.
10. "Grab a clamp instead. That way you have full control of this small piece." [BV · 4 beginner projects · 1:20 · 4.9x]
    ✎ **Shape:** hold small pieces with a clamp, never by hand. In the source it follows his own hole-saw injury, which can't be borrowed → "Clamp a piece this small before the hole saw touches it; a hand is never the clamp."
11. "Adding a bit of glue to the feet helps seal the exposed end grain from sucking up the moisture from the ground." [Voss · I still don't understand · 4:28 · 8.3x]
    ✓ **Shape:** a durability tip tied to where the product will live.
12. "Just make sure you are buying a dedicated pot cuz you're not going to want to make mac and cheese in this later." [Voss · Sawdust · 0:43 · 11.5x]
    ✓ **Shape:** keep equipment used on the product out of food use, with the everyday reason.
13. "Either way, just make sure you have a sacrificial piece under the pieces that you're drilling to prevent any kind of tear out." [BV · student loan · 5:31 · 5.6x]
    ✓ **Shape:** a backer piece under the work, with what it prevents.
14. "Make sure to spread that glue like you were spreading butter on toast…" [BV · Truck · 4:35 · 39.4x]
    ✓ **Shape:** an everyday comparison that shows how much and how thin. A comparison, not a joke.
15. "Just make sure you always keep your wigglies away from that spinny thing." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 0:54 · 9.2x]
    ✗ A recurring BV catchphrase (it turns up in other videos too), and competitors' signature lines are banned. The safety point survives in plain words: "Keep your hands well clear of the blade."

## 6. Candor
Real tradeoffs, limits and catches, said plainly. Never an invented mishap.

1. "I'm being honest, 10 bucks does seem a little steep for these nails, but it is what it is." [BV · Truck · 0:32 · 39.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** honest about a price that stings.
2. "The magic happens a little slower on these larger projects." [Voss · ZERO CUTS · 5:17 · 4.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a real tradeoff that grows with the size of the piece.
3. "This method gives you access to any color but honestly doesn't turn out too bad." [Voss · ZERO CUTS · 3:48 · 4.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a modest, believable verdict on a method.
4. "It creates additional pitch and resin on my blades, the boards are heavier and ugly, plus the chemicals aren't great to be around." [Voss · I still don't understand · 4:39 · 8.3x]
   ✓ **Shape:** an opinion against a material, with reasons (here, treated lumber).
5. "Problem being, this is gigantic and going to eat our profits 100% away." [Voss · Sawdust · 3:39 · 11.5x]
   ✓ **Shape:** names the catch in a plan before moving to the better option.
6. "Um, it's got some problems." [Voss · This ONE Project · 3:46 · 10.0x]
   ✗ This needs a real jig that went wrong on a real bench. Never invent one.
7. "Now, when it comes to the electric bill, the insurance, and all that, that gets more in depth of the business side of things." [BV · Truck · 10:37 · 39.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** says plainly which costs the simple math leaves out of scope.
8. "Now, being that we've got a long grain glue to an end grain, that is going to fail over time." [BV · Non stop orders · 6:35 · 6.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** names a weak joint, then the fix follows straight away (here, dowels across it).
9. "And then it's just a matter of a little bit of sanding or maybe a lot of sanding." [BV · sell fast · 2:44 · 11.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** an understatement corrected on the spot, owning the tedious part.
10. "Now, when it comes to fastening these longer sides, I'm not going to lie, it can get kind of tricky. So, if you have longer clamps, make sure to use them." [BV · 32 products · 13:50 · 7.1x]
   ✓ **Shape:** warns that a step is fiddly, then gives the aid.
11. "People are putting their mouths on them and stuff. I just don't want to deal with that and waiting for it to cure and find the right products." [Voss · This ONE Project · 8:30 · 10.0x]
   ✎ **Shape:** leaving a stage out on purpose because of how the piece gets used. Make it an opinion with the safety reason → "I'd leave these bare. Anything that goes in a mouth needs a food-safe finish and a full cure, and on a whistle it isn't worth it."
12. "If you wanted to use old candles or you go to the thrift store, you pick up a whole bunch of used candles for cheap. However, those will have an odor, and you also have to deal with the glass and the wicks." [Voss · Sawdust · 2:31 · 11.5x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the cheap shortcut, then its hidden hassle.
13. "After doing a little trial and error with the first one, I was able to do the other four fairly quick." [BV · student loan · 11:51 · 5.6x]
   ✎ **Shape:** the first one is the slow one. Drop the claimed history → "Expect the first knot to take a few tries. Once the method clicks, the rest go quickly."
14. "These don't look too good now, but let's trust the process." [BV · wife · 6:46 · 12.7x]
   ✎ **Shape:** admits the piece looks rough partway through. "These … now" points at footage, so name the object → "The screw heads look rough at this stage. The plugs cover them later."
15. "I'm not too worried about it being out in the weather because it's right up under my porch." [BV · So many orders · 10:39 · 8.6x]
   ✎ **Shape:** where the piece holds up and where it won't. The porch is his own; say it as a limit → "Spar urethane is fine under a covered porch. Left out in full weather, plan on refinishing it."

## 7. Money

**Listing proof:**
- "If you look online, most of these go for a range of $25 per pumpkin." [BV · Truck · 9:26 · 39.4x]
  ✎ **Shape:** one typical price from the listings. Keep it, and word it as "listed at" unless there's real sales evidence.
- "I see these online and on Etsy going anywhere from a range of $48 upwards of 70 bucks." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 10:07 · 9.2x]
  ✎ **Shape:** a low-to-high range on a named platform. Same fix: "listed between $48 and $70 on Etsy."
- "But I want you to look at what these Etsy sellers are posting their items for and selling them for." [BV · wife · 9:19 · 12.7x]
  ✓ **Shape:** the cue for the listing screenshot.
- "This thing is in 32 people's carts and 35 have been sold in the last 24 hours." [BV · 32 products · 0:24 · 7.1x]
  ✓ **Shape:** cart and recent-sale counts read off a live listing. "Sold" is fair here only because the listing shows the count; name the platform so the editor can place the screenshot.

**The narrator's price:**
- "As far as mine goes, I'll wind up posting mine on my Etsy for about 40." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 10:46 · 9.2x]
  ✎ **Shape:** the narrator's own number. Make it an opinion with no shop claim: "I'd list them around $40."
- "I see some of these pumpkins going for upwards of $50 per. Yeah, right." [BV · student loan · 12:27 · 5.6x]
  ✎ **Shape:** doubt the top listing out loud, then a lower, realistic ask (he follows with "$20 … I think that's doable"). → "A few are listed as high as $50. I wouldn't plan on that; around $20 is a realistic ask."

**Cost:**
- "With the screws, the stain, and some paint, we're going to bring that total to $14.12 spent." [BV · wife · 9:02 · 12.7x]
  ✓ **Shape:** consumables added in.
- "Bringing our grand total to $7.90 in on this project." [BV · student loan · 12:19 · 5.6x]
  ✓ **Shape:** the one-line grand total.
- "Cost was $18.31 to build the nice one with the scorch paint and the Mod Podge, the finishes, everything." [Voss · ZERO CUTS · 11:06 · 4.0x]
  ✓ **Shape:** an itemized total for the dressed-up version.
- "This thing cost me right around $13 and some change, which is about the same exact cost of a Quarter Pounder meal from McDonald's." [BV · So many orders · 0:31 · 8.6x]
  ✎ **Shape:** cost compared to an everyday purchase. Drop "cost me" and the brand: "about thirteen bucks, roughly a fast-food meal."
- "$833.58 cents is our total if you have to buy all of your shop tools. If you already have some tools sitting around, $13.81 cents." [Voss · This ONE Project · 8:38 · 10.0x]
  ✓ **Shape:** two totals, with the tools and without, so the tools read as a one-time cost kept out of the per-piece figure.

**What's left, and scale:**
- "32 time 30, that's $960." [BV · 32 products · 5:17 · 7.1x]
  ✎ **Shape:** yield times price. Make it conditional: "if all 32 sell at $30."
- "That doesn't cover the cost of sitting at the craft booth or getting the craft booth or listing the product." [Voss · ZERO CUTS · 12:08 · 4.0x]
  ✓ **Shape:** honest about the costs the simple math leaves out.

**Listing angle (how to present it for sale):**
- "You'll be making six of these risers, so feel free to market four of them as a step stool." [BV · wife · 8:49 · 12.7x]
  ✓ **Shape:** the same piece listed under a second use.
- "Or what I like to market these as is a display station." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 9:59 · 9.2x]
  ✓ **Shape:** a better name for the listing. Works as an opinion.

## 8. The doubter
The viewer's own doubt said out loud, then answered.

1. "…if you jump in the comments saying, 'No one's going to buy that for $6.' If you don't believe in your product, nobody will believe in it, because you're the one that has to sell it to them." [Voss · This ONE Project · 10:31 · 10.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the strongest one: voice the doubt, then turn it.
2. "Well, Daniel, don't forget about the cost of your drill bits or your drill and your sanders and all that." [BV · Truck · 10:13 · 39.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a named imaginary doubter raising a fair cost. Whether to name one is a persona-profile decision.
3. "Nobody's going to buy them for that price. Just save you guys the comment." [Voss · Sawdust · 7:53 · 11.5x]
   ✓ **Shape:** concede a limit before the comments do.
4. "Before you hit the comment section, I do not have a build video on how to make this tote little slidey doohickey cart thing because I don't need to." [Voss · I still don't understand · 7:24 · 8.3x]
   ✓ **Shape:** pre-empt the obvious comment.
5. "And I say, 'Well, to some this might seem overpriced, but to those who value a personal, handmade, locally built piece of artwork, the price is perfect.'" [Voss · never had trouble selling · 12:48 · 0.4x]
   ✎ **Shape:** answer "overpriced" with what the buyer values. The customer exchange is his own story; the answer itself transfers as an opinion.
6. "Look, if you're going to be a woodworker, once you purchase your drill and your drill bits, you're set." [BV · Truck · 10:22 · 39.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the answer to the tool-cost doubt: tools are bought once and paid off over many batches.
7. "You might be asking yourself, 'Hey Marcus, didn't you just make 1x2s? Why don't you just buy those in the first place?'" [Voss · This ONE Project · 1:47 · 10.0x]
   ✎ **Shape:** the "why not just buy it ready-made?" question, answered with the price gap. Drop the name gag (no jokes) → "Why rip strips when 1x2s sit on the same shelf? A ripped 2x4 runs [pack price]; the ready-made strips run [pack price]."
8. "Well, okay, Daniel, they look good, but do they amplify? Let's find out." [BV · 32 products · 5:47 · 7.1x]
   ✎ **Shape:** the doubter asks whether it actually works. The answer here is a filmed test, which a persona can't claim; answer from the pack instead → "Does the slot really make a phone louder? [Pack source] says it does, by about [figure]."
9. "Now to be fair, they built theirs out of cedar. However, cedar's just another softwood." [BV · wife · 9:29 · 12.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** concede that the proof isn't like-for-like before anyone else can, then size the gap.
10. "By now, you've come to the conclusion that at the end of the day, you don't want a bunch of wax in the bottom of your fire pit, but that's not how this works because of science, it actually dries as a powder once it's burned up." [Voss · Sawdust · 6:35 · 11.5x]
   ✓ **Shape:** voice the viewer's practical worry, then settle it with a fact (the fact must trace to the pack).
11. "And just remember, I'm here to share some ideas and give you the data. And the data is what the data is." [BV · student loan · 13:08 · 5.6x]
   ✎ **Shape:** send the doubter to the numbers instead of arguing. → "Don't take my word on the price. The listings are up on screen; check them yourself."
12. "Let's say you have no shop, no tools, no experience. So, let's get you up to speed." [Voss · This ONE Project · 0:09 · 10.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** start from the doubter's worst case (nothing at all) and build up from there.

## 9. Adversaries
SKILL.md allows four, as categories only: the doubter, the big box store's markup, scammers and overpriced materials. One per video, two at most.

1. "The big box store thinks that they're selling you construction grade lumber when in all reality, they're actually selling you a secret furniture grade wood." [BV · credit cards · 3:46 · 3.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the big box store as a category, turned into a buying tip (hidden value on the shelf).
2. "I never go with that expensive ass pine select. It's like twice the cost of this regular naughty pine." [BV · hotcakes · 0:41 · 15.8x]
   ✓ **Shape:** overpriced materials, with one mild swear aimed at the price. ("Naughty" is the caption's spelling of knotty.)
3. "…all of the major big box stores are flooding in with Christmas garbage." [Voss · $100/Hour · 12:52 · 1.1x]
   ✓ **Shape:** category plus season. Mass-produced decor is the opening for handmade.
4. "Don't get scammed." [Voss · This Facebook order · 8:05 · 1.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** scammers, in three words.
5. "Speaking of not being fancy, there's absolutely nothing fancy about a 2x4x8 from your big box store. So, most likely, you're going to need to check for that square edge, and if it's not square, go ahead and make it so." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 0:20 · 9.2x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a jab at big box stock quality, turned straight into a check-it step.
6. "Or you could buy the whole sheet, like a 4x8 sheet, but that thing's $33, so save yourself some money if you're not cutting that big of a piece and triple up on these little squares." [BV · student loan · 6:57 · 5.6x]
   ✓ **Shape:** overpriced materials as "don't pay for the big unit you won't use."
7. "…the miter saw box because it's cheaper to actually buy the two pieces separate than to buy it as a pack." [Voss · I buy ALL the tools · 1:12 · 4.2x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the store bundle costs more than its parts (big box markup, as a buying tip).
8. "…cuz not everybody wants to spend eight kajillion dollars on totes for their organization." [Voss · I still don't understand · 5:07 · 8.3x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the pricey store-bought alternative the build replaces, aimed at the price.
9. "They're just buying these, folks. Buying these and selling them for way higher." [Voss · ZERO CUTS · 11:36 · 4.0x]
   ✎ **Shape:** the markup on mass-made pieces. Here it's aimed at the sellers, a group of people (retired). Aim it at the markup and only with pack support → "A lot of what's listed is factory-made and marked way up. Built by hand, the same piece costs [pack cost]."
10. "I really just wanted to show you guys what it looked like to literally can't sell these fast enough and all the click baits that you see on YouTube." [Voss · This ONE Project · 10:17 · 10.0x]
   ✗ Clickbait YouTube is a retired adversary.
11. "I need y'all to smack that like button and share this content so we can beat this algorithm." [BV · 32 products · 4:27 · 7.1x]
   ✗ "The algorithm" is retired, and this one sits inside a CTA.
12. "What? I don't know about y'all, but I'd much rather buy some wood than that garbage." [BV · hotcakes · 0:23 · 15.8x]
   ✗ "That garbage" is a named fast-food chain's meal, named one line earlier: a named-company negative. What survives is the everyday-price comparison without the jab (group 7, Cost).
13. "But don't forget the taxman. He's going to want to get his cut, too." [BV · wife · 9:10 · 12.7x]
   ✗ The taxman isn't on the list. The fact survives as a plain money-block line: taxes come out of what's left.

## 10. Where to sell
Venue, season and logistics, matched to the product.

1. "It's an easy sell on Facebook Marketplace, cost-friendly to ship on Etsy, and its ability to be personalized is why you can name your price." [Voss · ZERO CUTS · 0:01 · 4.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** matches the product's traits to each venue.
2. "…wall-mounted hangers can do extremely well at the local markets and online." [BV · sell fast · 11:09 · 11.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** one plain line naming both venues.
3. "If you're selling them online, now you're competing with anything else available online." [Voss · Sawdust · 8:03 · 11.5x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the honest downside of a venue.
4. "Just like the planter boxes, I only sell these on Facebook Marketplace. That way, I can offer free local pickup, delivery if they want to pay for it." [Voss · I still don't understand · 6:51 · 8.3x]
   ✎ **Shape:** a bulky piece belongs on a local venue. The reasons transfer and the personal habit doesn't: "Bulky, so it's a Marketplace item: free local pickup, delivery for a fee, and nothing to haul to a booth."
5. "It is no secret that when the springtime comes around the local markets get flooded with planners and super oversaturated." [BV · Non stop orders · 0:14 · 6.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the venue is saturated with one product, so bring a different one. ("Planners" is the caption's spelling of planters.)
6. "But it all boils down to your demographics and where you're selling at." [BV · student loan · 12:38 · 5.6x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the venue sets the price, not the piece alone.
7. "These are easy to fit into vehicles, not only just trucks, but people can get them home a lot simpler, and they seem to do very well." [Voss · I still don't understand · 6:29 · 8.3x]
   ✎ **Shape:** size the piece so a local buyer can haul it home. "They seem to do very well" is a sales claim → "At four feet it fits in the back of a hatchback, so a Marketplace buyer doesn't need a truck."
8. "Now, for mine, I'm going to stage it real nice and try and get some shots of the birds in it, and put it on my Etsy for around 45, maybe 50 bucks." [BV · So many orders · 10:29 · 8.6x]
   ✎ **Shape:** photograph it in use for the online listing. Drop the shop claim → "For an Etsy listing, shoot it hanging outside with birds on it, not sitting on a bench."
9. "And during the fall, these things are stupid popular." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 10:24 · 9.2x]
   ✓ **Shape:** name the product's selling season.
10. "You can sell it as an animal bedding, horses, goats, chickens." [Voss · Sawdust · 8:46 · 11.5x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a second buyer for the leftovers. Add the safety line: only sawdust from untreated, unfinished solid wood goes to animals.
11. "Pretty simple, but you're going to throw the scrap away anyway and if it gets somebody to buy from your booth for the first time, success." [Voss · never had trouble selling · 1:47 · 0.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a cheap scrap item as the booth's door-opener.

## 11. The final content beat (before the end CTA)

1. "I think the big takeaway, maybe don't make 170 of them. Try like 20." [Voss · This ONE Project · 9:59 · 10.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a practical, honest scale-down.
2. "And above all else, you have to believe in your product, and you have to believe in the price you're selling it for…" [Voss · This ONE Project · 10:26 · 10.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** the doubter, turned into a closing belief.
3. "…it is indeed your turn to get in your shop and make some sawdust." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 11:24 · 9.2x]
   ✗ BV's signature sign-off, in nearly every BV video. Never borrow a competitor's catchphrase; the persona's own sign-off comes from the persona profile.
4. "Now is the perfect time to make these projects, especially being fall with Halloween and Thanksgiving coming around the corner." [BV · Truck · 10:52 · 39.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a seasonal push: why now.
5. "I did a little bit of research and you can research this, too, that people are selling these like hot cakes. It's definitely a trend that I'm going to be hopping on and you should too." [BV · hotcakes · 9:11 · 15.8x]
   ✎ **Shape:** a trend verdict plus "check it yourself." "Selling like hot cakes" needs sales evidence and "hopping on" implies a shop → "Look the listings up yourself: there are plenty of them, and the asking prices are healthy. That's a trend I'd get in on."
6. "I highly recommend giving this one a shot. It's super easy and can be built out of whatever kind of material you want to use." [BV · sell fast · 10:58 · 11.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a straight recommendation plus "any wood works."
7. "Now, my job is to show you how to make certain items. Your job is to build them and sell them." [BV · Non stop orders · 10:36 · 6.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** hand the job over to the viewer.
8. "I made six for my wife, but when she shared them with her Facebook following and shared them with a couple of local crafters, I started getting so many orders for these." [BV · wife · 9:54 · 12.7x]
   ✗ Family and orders as the closing proof. The persona has neither; never invent them.
9. "Now, one thing I did forget to mention is if you want to get away from using that 50° bevel, just use a 45° bevel, and that way that's the only bevel you'll have to use for the whole project." [BV · So many orders · 11:09 · 8.6x]
   ✎ **Shape:** a last simplifying tip. Here it's an afterthought tacked on after the sign-off; a script places it before the CTA, with no "forgot" → "One shortcut: run every bevel at 45 and skip the 50 altogether. It still closes up."
10. "So, what else could you do with your sawdust to make a quick buck? Really depends on how much sawdust you're trucking out of your garage each week." [Voss · Sawdust · 8:31 · 11.5x]
   ✓ **Shape:** widen out to other uses of the same input.
11. "If you're just not a big fan of the clipboard sellers, get yourself some bottle opener hardware and use that instead." [BV · 4 beginner projects · 18:43 · 4.9x]
   ✓ **Shape:** swap the hardware for a different product off the same blank.
12. "However, with access to the internet at your fingertips, you shouldn't have any kind of problem marketing yourself, building yourself a brand, that way you can make a few extra bucks from doing your hobby, just like me." [BV · student loan · 12:55 · 5.6x]
   ✎ **Shape:** reassure the viewer they can reach buyers. "Shouldn't have any kind of problem" is close to a guarantee and "just like me" is claimed history → "You don't need a tourist town. An online listing reaches buyers well past your own zip code."
13. "That's still pretty good. It's a pretty crazy product for not any work." [Voss · ZERO CUTS · 12:15 · 4.0x]
   ✎ **Shape:** a plain verdict right after the caveat. "For not any work" overstates → "Even after those costs, it's a fair return for a short build."
14. "So in that case, you sell one, you've made more money than the US governor of Maine." [Voss · 19 products · 4:27 · 9.2x]
   ✗ A joke built on a salary comparison. No jokes, no income framing.
15. "And you're building this from one 2 by 4." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 11:13 · 9.2x]
   ✓ **Shape:** restate the small input against the result. Keep the money line before it conditional.

## 12. Hook-to-first-material transitions

The line that carries the viewer out of the promise and into the first board or the first cut. Read with group 1 (promise) and group 2 (materials).

1. "…you'll be able to buy yourself an airline ticket to anywhere you want to go. You're going to grab two boards totaling right around 12 bucks." [BV · wife · 0:05 · 12.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** hard cut. The sentence after the promise is the first material and its price, with no bridge at all. The tightest way to meet the 15-second rule.
2. "Let's go. Slide up to Lowe's and grab yourself a 1x4x8 for around eight bucks." [BV · hotcakes · 0:08 · 15.8x]
   ✎ **Shape:** a two-word launch beat between the promise and the store run. BV uses "Let's go" as the launch in many of his videos, so it's his signature: use the persona's own launch beat if the profile has one, or none → "Right, the board: one 1x4x8 from the big box store, about eight dollars."
3. "Speaking of not being fancy, there's absolutely nothing fancy about a 2x4x8 from your big box store." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 0:20 · 9.2x]
   ✎ **Shape:** echo pivot. The material line reuses a word from the hook. His hook word came from a brag about his own shop, so echo a word from the persona's promise line instead → if the promise said "no fancy tools": "The lumber's no fancier than the tools: one plain 2x4x8, the straightest one on the rack."
4. "Here's what you're going to need. One board, five masonry cut nails, some natural fiber rope, a few basic power tools, coffee included, and no fancy shop required." [BV · student loan · 0:04 · 5.6x]
   ✎ **Shape:** announced shopping list: a short header, then the whole kit in one breath. Cut the "coffee included" quip (no jokes) → "The full list: one 2x4, five cut nails, a length of natural rope and the basic tools. No shop needed."
5. "First ingredient you need is some sawdust. Take it out of your dust collection system." [Voss · Sawdust · 0:58 · 11.5x]
   ✓ **Shape:** recipe framing ("first ingredient," then "second ingredient") for builds whose inputs aren't lumber: wax, offcuts, hardware. Each ingredient gets its own short line and its source. Voss reached this line after a minute of jokes; the shape is the pivot, not the run-up.
6. "Let's say you have no shop, no tools, no experience. So, let's get you up to speed." [Voss · This ONE Project · 0:09 · 10.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** zero-start hypothetical, then the complete kit from pencils up. Fits titles that promise the build pays for its own tools; every tool price comes from the pack.
7. "For today's build, all you're going to need is a couple edge glued round panels." [Voss · ZERO CUTS · 0:33 · 4.0x]
   ✓ **Shape:** anti-list, then "all you need is." First a run of tools the build doesn't need, then the single material. His anti-list points at his wall ("any of these other tools hanging up"); name the tools instead.
8. "Damn, that's crazy. Let me show you how easy this thing is to get built." [BV · 32 products · 0:31 · 7.1x]
   ✎ **Shape:** proof figure → short reaction → ease promise → material. The figure before it (a listing's sales count) must be real evidence from the pack, and "let me show you" casts the narrator as the builder → "That's a busy listing for something this plain. All it takes is one 2x4."
9. "So, for our first project, I'm going to show you how to combat that…" [BV · Non stop orders · 0:22 · 6.4x]
   ✎ **Shape:** market glut → the version nobody else makes → material. The sentence before it says spring markets are flooded with one product; the next line is the board. The glut claim needs support in the pack, and "I'm going to show you" goes → "Spring tables fill up with the same planter, so build the one that looks different. It starts with one 2x10x8."
10. "…but don't worry, we're going to turn a profit. Measure halfway down your 2x4 and cut it in half." [Voss · This ONE Project · 1:09 · 10.0x]
    ✎ **Shape:** a worry answered in half a sentence, then straight into the first cut. "We're going to turn a profit" is a guarantee → "That total looks steep, and only sales pay it back. First cut: the 2x4 in half, at 48 inches."
11. "We need to cut our board into 16 different pieces. That's a lot, I know." [BV · Truck · 0:44 · 39.4x]
    ✓ **Shape:** the cut count plus a three-word concession, between the materials and the first measurement. Sets the size of the job before any step. (The same move flipped, "simple, I know," opens Voss's *raise my price* cuts.)
12. "And before we measure, we need to make sure that we have a square edge to measure from." [BV · credit cards · 0:37 · 3.4x]
    ✓ **Shape:** a prerequisite check between the board and the first measurement. Use it when the first real cut depends on it: a square end, a straight edge, a rough factory end.
13. "Grab a 2x4, your cordless drill and your miter saw; let's turn that $3 construction grade piece of garbage into $810." [Voss · 19 products · 0:08 · 9.2x]
    ✎ **Shape:** the kit as one imperative, with the money promise folded into the same sentence. $810 is stated as a sure thing → "One 2x4, a drill and a miter saw. That three-dollar board could add up to eight hundred, if every piece sells."
14. "I'm going to show you how to do the first one maybe the second one and then you guys just copycat it the rest of the way down the board…" [Voss · I buy ALL the tools · 2:15 · 4.2x]
    ✎ **Shape:** the batching plan, said before the first cut: the first piece in full, the rest by repetition. The first-person demo framing goes → "The first piece gets every step spelled out. After that, repeat it along the board until the board runs out."
15. "So, grab a 2x4 and that box of nails that you've been itching to find a purpose for." [Voss · 5 Minute Project · 0:44 · 3.6x]
    ✓ **Shape:** the material is something already sitting in the viewer's shop. Turns the materials line into a nod to the viewer's own stash.

## 13. Short bridges between steps

Brief connective lines that move the viewer from one build step to the next. The steps themselves are in group 4.

1. "Now, it's time to get our 16 pieces cut." [BV · Truck · 1:13 · 39.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** "it's time to" plus the job and its count. Announces the next stage in under ten words.
2. "This is where the cut nails come into play." [BV · Truck · 8:43 · 39.4x]
   ✓ **Shape:** payoff callback: a material bought in the opening finally gets used. Only works if the materials block named it.
3. "Now that we've got these two pieces cleaned up, we'll set them to the side for now." [BV · hotcakes · 5:24 · 15.8x]
   ✓ **Shape:** result, then park it. Closes one part and clears the bench for the next.
4. "These don't look too good now, but let's trust the process." [BV · wife · 6:46 · 12.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** admit the ugly middle stage, then promise it resolves. Name what looks rough (the screw heads, the glue lines) so the visual matches.
5. "And then it's just a matter of a little bit of sanding or maybe a lot of sanding." [BV · sell fast · 2:44 · 11.7x]
   ✓ **Shape:** play it down, then correct it honestly in the same breath. Candor doing a bridge's job.
6. "And we'll let this sit for about 15 minutes and I'll meet you back here." [BV · sell fast · 9:34 · 11.7x]
   ✎ **Shape:** clock skip: a wait, with its length. "I'll meet you back here" is a presenter's line → "Give the glue fifteen minutes before the next part goes on."
7. "Now, our next order of business is going to be over here at the router table…" [BV · Non stop orders · 2:39 · 6.4x]
   ✎ **Shape:** "next order of business" plus the tool. "Over here" points into a shop → "Next order of business is the router." A router is beyond the standard kit, so the step after it gives the alternative.
8. "Now, while we let those pieces dry, we're going to be productive and get our next set of four cut." [BV · 2 week Vacation · 5:11 · 9.2x]
   ✓ **Shape:** use the wait: the drying time becomes time for the next cuts. Keeps a glue-up from stalling the video.
9. "And we've got all of our side pieces cut. Time for some pocket holes." [BV · 32 products · 10:42 · 7.1x]
   ✓ **Shape:** a status line, then a five-word heading for the next step. (A pocket-hole jig is beyond the standard kit, so the next line gives the alternative.)
10. "And this will all make sense shortly." [BV · Non stop orders · 1:25 · 6.4x]
    ✗ A small retention tease: it holds back the reason for a step. What survives: give the reason now ("those marks are where the grooves go").
11. "Now, back to the build." [BV · 4 beginner projects · 6:38 · 4.9x]
    ✓ **Shape:** a five-word return line after an aside (his was a store-run story). In these scripts the aside is a tip, a candor line or the mid CTA; the return is the same move.
12. "18 1/2 pieces later, we have our finished project." [Voss · I buy ALL the tools · 5:53 · 4.2x]
    ✓ **Shape:** count skip: the repeats collapse into a number, then the result. The count must come from the pack's cut list.
13. "Now, what if we could pump up the aesthetics and also pump up the price?" [Voss · ZERO CUTS · 3:16 · 4.0x]
    ✓ **Shape:** a question that bridges from the finished basic version into an optional upgrade step, and ties the extra step to money.
14. "We are finally on to the assembly stage." [Voss · Truly Woven · 5:55 · 2.7x]
    ✓ **Shape:** stage marker: names the phase, not the action, after a long run of cutting and sanding.

## 14. Finish lines

Lines from the finish stage: final sanding, stain, paint, oil, sealer, burning, distressing, drying.

1. "Yes, that is absolutely true. However, most projects that I do with pine, I'm going to be looking to make it rustic, so it really doesn't apply in this instance." [BV · Truck · 7:58 · 39.4x]
   ✎ **Shape:** concede the textbook step (here, wood conditioner before stain), then say why this piece skips it. "Most projects that I do" is personal history → "Conditioner evens out stain on pine. On a rustic piece the blotches are the look, so skip it here."
2. "I'm using some of this red mahogany stain, and it's oil based, so I'll put about two to three coats on it, wiping down between each coat." [BV · hotcakes · 7:48 · 15.8x]
   ✎ **Shape:** finish type → number of coats → what happens between coats, in one line. Make it an instruction → "Oil-based stain gets two or three coats; wipe each one down before the next."

## 15. Mid-video CTAs

Shape only. Each line is quoted for reference; the note covers placement, length, the ask and the return. The offer, its wording and its location always come from the persona profile, and the mechanics from core `cta-and-endings.md`: one mid-video CTA, after the first real payoff, one ask, what it is, what it adds beyond this video, where it is, then a return line.

1. "There are only 47% of my viewers that are subscribed. So, if you're not subscribed to the channel, consider doing so." [BV · Truck · 6:01 · 39.4x]
   ✎ **Placement:** after all the cuts and the first finished glue-up, about 55% in. **Shape:** a figure about the audience, a conditional ask, then a second ask stacked on; it returns with the reason for the next step. No added-value promise and two asks → "[What the persona's offer is], with [what it adds beyond this video]. It's [where it is]. Next, [the next step]."
2. "Turning eyeballs into potential buyers is sort of like turning viewers into subscribers." [BV · hotcakes · 2:19 · 15.8x]
   ✎ **Placement:** right after the first drilling step, the first real step, about a quarter in. **Shape:** an analogy from the video's subject to the ask, then the ask; the return line names the next mark. Keep the analogy device and swap the ask → "[How this piece wins a buyer] is how [the persona's offer] works too: [what it adds]. [Where it is]. Now, [the next step]."
3. "I hope that you can find some time to drop down below and hit that thumbs up button. It really helps." [BV · hotcakes · 7:35 · 15.8x]
   ✎ **Placement:** between the last sanding and the stain, near the end of the build; his second ask in the video. **Shape:** a one-to-two sentence ask wedged between two steps, with the next step as the return line. The persona gets one mid-video CTA, so use the wedge-and-return form at the first payoff → "[The persona's offer]: [what it adds], [where it is]. Now, [the next step]."
4. "I'll be batching out three for this project. And while I do this, I've got a huge favor to ask." [BV · sell fast · 3:27 · 11.7x]
   ✎ **Placement:** right after the first piece is complete, while the rest are batched: the first-payoff spot SKILL asks for. **Shape:** the ask plays over repetitive batching, then returns with the finish step. The narrator isn't doing the batching → "While the other [number] get cut out: [the persona's offer and what it adds], [where it is]. Then [the next step]."
5. "If you fancy that push stick keeping my hand toes far away from that sharp spinny blade, I have free downloadable plans for all the popular push sticks used by the kings of YouTube." [Voss · This ONE Project · 1:36 · 10.0x]
   ✎ **Placement:** during the first rip cuts, right after the materials. **Shape:** a one-sentence conditional offer triggered by an object in the current step; the build carries on without a pause. Rewrite only if the real offer covers that object → "If [the item in this step] would help, [the persona's offer] has [the related extra]; it's [where it is]."
6. "If you download the free printable plans, you'll find the 47-in version with instructions and measurements. You'll also find a 96-in version where I use two full-length 2 by 4s for the long sides, and then there's only one leg in the center." [Voss · I still don't understand · 5:46 · 8.3x]
   ✎ **Placement:** inside the money block, after the profit math and before where to sell. **Shape:** a conditional followed by a contents list that includes something the video doesn't cover: the core rule's added-value promise in its plainest form. It returns into the reasons for the size it sells. Move it to the first payoff and keep the contents list → "[The persona's offer] has [contents], plus [what this video leaves out]. It's [where it is]. Now, [the next step]."
7. "And before we continue, be sure to leave a like to help support the channel." [BV · 4 beginner projects · 0:22 · 4.9x]
   ✗ **Placement:** 26 seconds in, before the first cut, with nothing yet delivered. A pause-before-content ask breaks give-before-asking; nothing survives.
8. "Just a friendly reminder from yours truly, there are going to be plans available and I will link them in the pinned comments." [BV · 32 products · 12:57 · 7.1x]
   ✎ **Placement:** late, between the torch finish and the edge profile on his second project, with no return line. **Shape:** one sentence, offer plus location, introduced as a reminder. Keep the one-sentence form, add the value line and a return, and place it at the first payoff → "[The persona's offer]: [what it adds], at [where it is]. Back to [the next step]."
9. "I need y'all to smack that like button and share this content so we can beat this algorithm." [BV · 32 products · 4:27 · 7.1x]
   ✗ The ask is framed against a retired adversary (the platform's algorithm), stacks two asks, and came under a minute after his first ask. Nothing survives beyond the reminder that a CTA never names an adversary.

Keep the question opener with one ask only, and move it to the first payoff → "Got [the persona's offer] yet? It has [what it adds]; [where it is]. Now, [the next step]."

Later than SKILL's first-payoff spot; keep the location-first order → "[Where it is] has [the persona's offer]: [what it adds], because [why it helps with this build]. Now, [the next step]."

Keep the label-and-exit frame; the ask itself was a platform feature → "[Short label]. [The persona's offer and what it adds], [where it is]. [A fixed exit line back to the build]."
